title: Students Can't Focus
author: Patrick Dempsey
summary: Education blames student attention problems on TikTok and social media while simultaneously structuring the entire learning experience around planned interruptions and constant context-switching. Students move between four to five unrelated courses every 50 minutes, receive feedback after their active engagement has ended, and are never allowed to stay with any problem long enough for deep engagement to develop. Colleges possess all the physical, intellectual, and relational infrastructure needed to create extraordinary conditions for sustained focus—but choose a Monday/Wednesday/Friday grid instead. The natural consequence of this system is not distracted students—it's students who've learned the only rational response: finish what's due, submit the product, collect the grade, and move on. AI thrives in exactly this kind of shallow, disconnected, frequently-interrupted environment. Education has externalized the attention problem while designing it into the system.
points: The entire student experience is organized around planned interruptions—50-minute periods, five simultaneous courses, feedback arriving after engagement ends—while blaming TikTok for the fragmentation that design creates.
Deep engagement requires entering a problem slowly, tolerating apparent non-progress, and returning repeatedly—precisely what the semester grid prevents.
AI thrives in shallow, disconnected, frequently-interrupted work environments—the exact environment education has built; this is not coincidence.
The tools for sustained attention (labs, studios, libraries, faculty, peers) exist in higher education; the schedule systematically destroys their potential.
Sustained attention has become a moral demand placed on students rather than an environmental condition created for them—a fundamental abdication of institutional responsibility.
quotes: The institution blames students for failing to sustain an attention it intentionally makes almost impossible to sustain.
We seem to assume that attention can be started and stopped on command.

An education serious about learning would create far more opportunities for sustained attention, appropriately difficult work, rapid interaction with the consequences of decisions, and—perhaps quite radically—the possibility of flow.
finish what is due, submit the required product, collect the grade, and move on.
education has turned sustained attention into a moral demand we make of students rather than a condition we create for them.

The point is, we say we want students deeply engaged in learning, while organizing nearly every part of their education to prevent them from remaining with anything long enough for deep engagement to occur.
